					<div id="mw-content-text" class="mw-body-content"><div class="mw-subjectpageheader">
</div><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Disk encryption software for Microsoft Windows</div>
<p class="mw-empty-elt">

</p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1358324954">@media(min-width:640px){.mw-parser-output .infobox{margin-left:1em;float:right;clear:right;width:22em}}.mw-parser-output nowrap;">Other names</th><td class="infobox-data">Device Encryption</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Programmer" title="Programmer">Developer</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Microsoft" title="Microsoft">Microsoft</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;">Initial release</th><td class="infobox-data">November&#160;30, 2006<span class="noprint">&#59;&#32;19 years ago</span><span style="display:none">&#160;(<span class="bday dtstart published updated">2006-11-30</span>)</span></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Operating_system" title="Operating system">Operating system</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Windows_Vista" title="Windows Vista">Windows Vista</a> and later</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Software_categories#Categorization_approaches" title="Software categories">Type</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Disk_encryption_software" title="Disk encryption software">Disk encryption software</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;">Website</th><td class="infobox-data"><span class="url"><a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/data-protection/bitlocker/">learn<wbr />.microsoft<wbr />.com<wbr />/en-us<wbr />/windows<wbr />/security<wbr />/operating-system-security<wbr />/data-protection<wbr />/bitlocker<wbr />/</a></span>&#160;<span class="penicon autoconfirmed-show"><span class="mw-valign-text-top" typeof="mw:File/Frameless"><a href="https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q871861?uselang=en#P856" title="Edit this on Wikidata"><img alt="Edit this on Wikidata" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/8a/OOjs_UI_icon_edit-ltr-progressive.svg/20px-OOjs_UI_icon_edit-ltr-progressive.svg.png" decoding="async" width="10" height="10" class="mw-file-element" data-file-width="20" data-file-height="20" /></a></span></span></td></tr></tbody></table> 
<p><b>BitLocker</b> is a <a href="/wiki/Full_volume_encryption" class="mw-redirect" title="Full volume encryption">full volume encryption</a> feature included with <a href="/wiki/Microsoft_Windows" title="Microsoft Windows">Microsoft Windows</a> versions starting with <a href="/wiki/Windows_Vista" title="Windows Vista">Windows Vista</a>. It is designed to protect data by providing <a href="/wiki/Encryption" title="Encryption">encryption</a> for entire <a href="/wiki/Volume_(computing)" title="Volume (computing)">volumes</a>. By default, it uses the <a href="/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard" title="Advanced Encryption Standard">Advanced Encryption Standard</a> (AES) algorithm in <a href="/wiki/Cipher_block_chaining" class="mw-redirect" title="Cipher block chaining">cipher block chaining</a> (CBC) or "<a href="/wiki/Xor%E2%80%93encrypt%E2%80%93xor" title="Xor–encrypt–xor">xor–encrypt–xor</a> (XEX)<a href="/wiki/Disk_encryption_theory#XEX-based_tweaked-codebook_mode_with_ciphertext_stealing_(XTS)" title="Disk encryption theory">-based tweaked codebook mode with ciphertext stealing</a>" (XTS) mode<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win10New&#95;1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win10New-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> with a 128-<a href="/wiki/Bit" title="Bit">bit</a> or 256-bit <a href="/wiki/Key_(cryptography)" title="Key (cryptography)">key</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FAQ&#95;2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FAQ-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-AES-CBC&#95;3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AES-CBC-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> CBC is not used over the whole disk; it is applied to each individual <a href="/wiki/Disk_sector" title="Disk sector">sector</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-AES-CBC&#95;3-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-AES-CBC-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History">History</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: History"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>BitLocker originated as a part of Microsoft's <a href="/wiki/Next-Generation_Secure_Computing_Base" title="Next-Generation Secure Computing Base">Next-Generation Secure Computing Base</a> architecture in 2004 as a feature tentatively codenamed "Cornerstone"<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PdWinHEC20042&#95;4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PdWinHEC20042-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-PDC-Exclusive2&#95;5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PDC-Exclusive2-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and was designed to protect information on devices, particularly if a device was lost or stolen. Another feature, titled "Code Integrity Rooting", was designed to validate the integrity of Microsoft Windows boot and system files.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-PdWinHEC20042&#95;4-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-PdWinHEC20042-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> When used in conjunction with a compatible <a href="/wiki/Trusted_Platform_Module" title="Trusted Platform Module">Trusted Platform Module</a> (TPM), BitLocker can validate the integrity of boot and system files before decrypting a protected volume; an unsuccessful validation will prohibit access to a protected system.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-TechnicalOverview2&#95;6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TechnicalOverview2-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-ExecutiveOverview2&#95;7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ExecutiveOverview2-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> BitLocker was briefly called Secure Startup before Windows Vista's <a href="/wiki/Release_to_manufacturing" class="mw-redirect" title="Release to manufacturing">release to manufacturing</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-TechnicalOverview2&#95;6-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TechnicalOverview2-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>BitLocker is available on:
</p>
<ul><li><a href="/wiki/Windows_Vista_editions#Windows_Vista_Enterprise" title="Windows Vista editions">Enterprise</a> and <a href="/wiki/Windows_Vista_editions#Windows_Vista_Ultimate" title="Windows Vista editions">Ultimate</a> editions of <a href="/wiki/Windows_Vista" title="Windows Vista">Windows Vista</a> and <a href="/wiki/Windows_7" title="Windows 7">Windows 7</a></li>
<li>Pro and Enterprise editions of <a href="/wiki/Windows_8" title="Windows 8">Windows 8</a> and <a href="/wiki/Windows_8.1" title="Windows 8.1">8.1</a><sup id="cite&#95;ref-BitLockerNew&#95;8-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BitLockerNew-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-FAQ&#95;2-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FAQ-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Windows Embedded Standard 7 and Windows Thin PC</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/Windows_Server_2008" title="Windows Server 2008">Windows Server 2008</a><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Server2008&#95;9-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Server2008-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> and later<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Server2008R2&#95;10-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Server2008R2-10"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-BitLockerNew&#95;8-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BitLockerNew-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions of <a href="/wiki/Windows_10" title="Windows 10">Windows 10</a><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win10editions&#95;11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win10editions-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions of <a href="/wiki/Windows_11" title="Windows 11">Windows 11</a><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win11editions&#95;12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win11editions-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li></ul>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Features">Features</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Features"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1358324954" /><table class="infobox vevent"><tbody><tr><th colspan="2" class="infobox-above summary">manage-bde</th></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Programmer" title="Programmer">Developer</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Microsoft" title="Microsoft">Microsoft</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;">Initial release</th><td class="infobox-data">January&#160;30, 2007<span class="noprint">&#59;&#32;19 years ago</span><span style="display:none">&#160;(<span class="bday dtstart published updated">2007-01-30</span>)</span></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Operating_system" title="Operating system">Operating system</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Microsoft_Windows" title="Microsoft Windows">Microsoft Windows</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Software_categories#Categorization_approaches" title="Software categories">Type</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Command_(computing)" title="Command (computing)">Command</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Software_license" title="Software license">License</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Proprietary_software" title="Proprietary software">Proprietary</a> <a href="/wiki/Commercial_software" title="Commercial software">commercial software</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;">Website</th><td class="infobox-data"><a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/manage-bde">manage-bde</a></td></tr></tbody></table> 
<p>Initially, the graphical BitLocker interface in Windows Vista could only encrypt the <a href="/wiki/Operating_system" title="Operating system">operating system</a> volume.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-13" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Starting with Windows Vista with Service Pack 1 and Windows Server 2008, volumes other than the operating system volume could be encrypted using the graphical tool. Still, some aspects of the BitLocker (such as turning autolocking on or off) had to be managed through a command-line tool called <code>manage-bde.wsf</code>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>The version of BitLocker included in Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 Release 2 adds the ability to encrypt removable drives. On <a href="/wiki/Windows_XP" title="Windows XP">Windows XP</a> or Windows Vista, read-only access to these drives can be achieved through a program called BitLocker To Go Reader, if <a href="/wiki/FAT16" class="mw-redirect" title="FAT16">FAT16</a>, <a href="/wiki/FAT32" class="mw-redirect" title="FAT32">FAT32</a> or <a href="/wiki/ExFAT" title="ExFAT">exFAT</a> filesystems are used.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In addition, a new command-line tool called <code>manage-bde</code> replaced the old <code>manage-bde.wsf</code>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Starting with Windows Server 2012 and Windows 8, Microsoft has complemented BitLocker with the Microsoft Encrypted Hard Drive specification, which allows the cryptographic operations of BitLocker encryption to be offloaded to the storage device's hardware, for example, <a href="/wiki/Self-encrypting_drive" class="mw-redirect" title="Self-encrypting drive">self-encrypting drives</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-17" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-17"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>17<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-18" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-18"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>18<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> In addition, BitLocker can now be managed through <a href="/wiki/Windows_PowerShell" class="mw-redirect" title="Windows PowerShell">Windows PowerShell</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-19" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-19"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>19<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Finally, Windows 8 introduced <a href="/wiki/Windows_To_Go" title="Windows To Go">Windows To Go</a> in its Enterprise edition, which BitLocker can protect.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-20" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-20"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>20<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Device_encryption">Device encryption</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Device encryption"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p><a href="/wiki/Windows_Mobile_6.5" title="Windows Mobile 6.5">Windows Mobile 6.5</a>, <a href="/wiki/Windows_RT" title="Windows RT">Windows RT</a> and core editions of Windows 8.1 include <b>device encryption</b>, a feature-limited version of BitLocker that encrypts the whole system.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ars-deviceencryption2&#95;21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ars-deviceencryption2-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-22" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-22"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>22<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-HelpPortal2&#95;23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HelpPortal2-23"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Logging in with a <a href="/wiki/Microsoft_account" title="Microsoft account">Microsoft account</a> with administrative privileges automatically begins the encryption process. The recovery key is stored to either the Microsoft account or <a href="/wiki/Active_Directory" title="Active Directory">Active Directory</a> (Active Directory requires Pro editions of Windows), allowing it to be retrieved from any computer. While device encryption is offered on all editions of Windows 8.1, unlike BitLocker, device encryption requires that the device meet the <a href="/wiki/InstantGo" class="mw-redirect" title="InstantGo">InstantGo</a> (formerly <a href="/wiki/Connected_Standby" class="mw-redirect" title="Connected Standby">Connected Standby</a>) specifications,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-HelpPortal2&#95;23-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HelpPortal2-23"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>23<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> which requires <a href="/wiki/Solid-state_drive" title="Solid-state drive">solid-state drives</a> and a TPM 2.0 chip.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ars-deviceencryption2&#95;21-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ars-deviceencryption2-21"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>21<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-24" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-24"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>24<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Starting with Windows 10 1703, the requirements for device encryption have changed, requiring a TPM 1.2 or 2.0 module with PCR 7 support, <a href="/wiki/UEFI_Secure_Boot" class="mw-redirect" title="UEFI Secure Boot">UEFI Secure Boot</a>, and that the device meets Modern Standby requirements or HSTI validation.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>25<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Device encryption requirements were relaxed in Windows 11 24H2, with the Modern Standby, HSTI and Secure Boot compliance no longer required and the DMA interfaces blocklist removed.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-26" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-26"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>26<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> And device encryption will be enabled by default by clean installation of Windows 11 24H2, called <i>auto device encryption</i>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-27" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-27"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>27<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In September 2019 a new update was released (KB4516071<sup id="cite&#95;ref-28" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-28"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>28<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>) changing the default setting for BitLocker when encrypting a self-encrypting drive. Now, the default is to use software encryption for newly encrypted drives. This is due to hardware encryption flaws and security concerns related to those issues.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-29" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-29"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>29<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Encryption_modes">Encryption modes</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: Encryption modes"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Three authentication mechanisms can be used as building blocks to implement BitLocker encryption:<sup id="cite&#95;ref-30" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-30"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>30<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<ul><li><b>Transparent operation mode</b>:  This mode uses the capabilities of TPM 1.2 hardware to provide for transparent user experience—the user powers up and logs into Windows as usual. The key used for <a href="/wiki/Disk_encryption" title="Disk encryption">disk encryption</a> is sealed (encrypted) by the TPM chip and will only be released to the OS loader code if the early boot files appear to be unmodified. The pre-OS components of BitLocker achieve this by implementing a Static Root of Trust Measurement—a methodology specified by the <a href="/wiki/Trusted_Computing_Group" title="Trusted Computing Group">Trusted Computing Group</a> (TCG). This mode is vulnerable to a <a href="/wiki/Cold_boot_attack" title="Cold boot attack">cold boot attack</a>, as it allows a powered-down machine to be <a href="/wiki/Booting" title="Booting">booted</a> by an attacker. It is also vulnerable to a sniffing attack, as the volume encryption key is transferred in plain text from the TPM to the CPU during a successful boot.</li>
<li><b>User authentication mode</b>: This mode requires that the user provide some authentication to the pre-boot environment in the form of a pre-boot <a href="/wiki/Personal_identification_number" title="Personal identification number">PIN</a> or password.</li>
<li><b>USB Key Mode</b>: The user must insert a USB device that contains a startup key into the computer to be able to boot  the protected OS. Note that this mode requires that the BIOS on the  protected machine supports the reading of USB devices in the pre-OS  environment. BitLocker does not support smart cards for pre-boot authentication.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-31" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-31"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>31<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li></ul>
<p>The following combinations of the above authentication mechanisms are supported, all with an optional <a href="/wiki/Key_escrow" title="Key escrow">escrow</a> recovery key:
</p>
<ul><li>TPM only<sup id="cite&#95;ref-32" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-32"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>32<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>TPM + PIN<sup id="cite&#95;ref-33" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-33"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>33<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>TPM + PIN + USB Key<sup id="cite&#95;ref-34" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-34"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>34<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>TPM + USB Key<sup id="cite&#95;ref-35" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-35"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>35<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>USB Key<sup id="cite&#95;ref-36" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-36"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>36<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>Password only<sup id="cite&#95;ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>37<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li></ul>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Operation">Operation</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=5" title="Edit section: Operation"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>BitLocker is a <a href="/wiki/Volume_(computing)" title="Volume (computing)">logical volume</a> encryption system. (A volume spans part of a <a href="/wiki/Hard_disk_drive" title="Hard disk drive">hard disk drive</a>, the whole drive or more than one drive.) When enabled, TPM and BitLocker can ensure the integrity of the trusted boot path (e.g. BIOS and boot sector), in order to prevent most offline physical attacks and boot sector malware.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win7FAQ&#95;38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win7FAQ-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In order for BitLocker to encrypt the volume holding the operating system, at least two <a href="/wiki/NTFS" title="NTFS">NTFS</a>-formatted volumes are required: one for the operating system (usually C:) and another with a minimum size of 100&#160;MB, which remains unencrypted and <a href="/wiki/Booting" title="Booting">boots</a> the operating system.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win7FAQ&#95;38-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win7FAQ-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> (In case of Windows Vista and <a href="/wiki/Windows_Server_2008" title="Windows Server 2008">Windows Server 2008</a>, however, the volume's minimum size is 1.5 GB and must have a <a href="/wiki/Drive_letter" class="mw-redirect" title="Drive letter">drive letter</a>.)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-39" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-39"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>39<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Unlike previous versions of Windows, Vista's "diskpart" command-line tool includes the ability to shrink the size of an NTFS volume so that this volume may be created from already allocated space. A tool called the BitLocker Drive Preparation Tool is also available from Microsoft that allows an existing volume on Windows Vista to be shrunk to make room for a new boot volume and for the necessary <a href="/wiki/Bootstrapping_(computing)" class="mw-redirect" title="Bootstrapping (computing)">bootstrapping</a> files to be transferred to it.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-40" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-40"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>40<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Once an alternate boot partition has been created, the TPM module needs to be initialized (assuming that this feature is being used), after which the required disk-encryption key protection mechanisms such as TPM, PIN or <a href="/wiki/Usb_key" class="mw-redirect" title="Usb key">USB key</a> are configured.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ExamRef&#95;41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ExamRef-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The volume is then encrypted as a background task, something that may take a considerable amount of time with a large disk as every logical sector is read, encrypted and rewritten back to disk.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ExamRef&#95;41-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ExamRef-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The keys are only protected after the whole volume has been encrypted when the volume is considered secure.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-42" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-42"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>42<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> BitLocker uses a low-level device driver to encrypt and decrypt all file operations, making interaction with the encrypted volume transparent to applications running on the platform.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ExamRef&#95;41-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ExamRef-41"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>41<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Encrypting_File_System" title="Encrypting File System">Encrypting File System</a> (EFS) may be used in conjunction with BitLocker to provide protection once the operating system is running. Protection of the files from processes and users within the operating system can only be performed using encryption software that operates within Windows, such as EFS. BitLocker and EFS, therefore, offer protection against different classes of attacks.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-43" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-43"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>43<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In Active Directory environments, BitLocker supports optional key escrow to Active Directory, although a schema update may be required for this to work (i.e. if the Active Directory Services are hosted on a Windows version previous to Windows Server 2008).
</p><p>BitLocker and other full disk encryption systems can be attacked by a <a href="/wiki/Bootkit" class="mw-redirect" title="Bootkit">rogue boot manager</a>. Once the malicious bootloader captures the secret, it can decrypt the Volume Master Key (VMK), which would then allow access to decrypt or modify any information on an encrypted hard disk. By configuring a TPM to protect the trusted boot pathway, including the <a href="/wiki/BIOS" title="BIOS">BIOS</a> and <a href="/wiki/Boot_sector" title="Boot sector">boot sector</a>, BitLocker can mitigate this threat. (Note that some non-malicious changes to the boot path may cause a <a href="/wiki/Trusted_Platform_Module#Platform_integrity" title="Trusted Platform Module">Platform Configuration Register</a> check to fail, and thereby generate a false warning.)<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win7FAQ&#95;38-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win7FAQ-38"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>38<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Security_concerns">Security concerns</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: Security concerns"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="TPM_alone_is_not_enough">TPM alone is not enough</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=7" title="Edit section: TPM alone is not enough"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The "Transparent operation mode" and "User authentication mode" of BitLocker use TPM hardware to detect whether there are unauthorized changes to the pre-boot environment, including the <a href="/wiki/BIOS" title="BIOS">BIOS</a> and <a href="/wiki/Master_boot_record" title="Master boot record">MBR</a>. If any unauthorized changes are detected, BitLocker requests a recovery key on a USB device. This cryptographic secret is used to decrypt the Volume Master Key (VMK) and allow the <a href="/wiki/Booting" title="Booting">bootup</a> process to continue.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-TPM-operation2&#95;44-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-TPM-operation2-44"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>44<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> However, TPM alone is not enough:
</p>
<ul><li>In February 2008, a group of security researchers published details of a so-called "<a href="/wiki/Cold_boot_attack" title="Cold boot attack">cold boot attack</a>" that allows full disk encryption systems such as BitLocker to be compromised by booting the machine from removable media, such as a USB drive, into another operating system, then <a href="/wiki/Core_dump" title="Core dump">dumping</a> the contents of pre-boot memory.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ColdBoot2&#95;45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ColdBoot2-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The attack relies on the fact that <a href="/wiki/Dynamic_random-access_memory" title="Dynamic random-access memory">DRAM</a> <a href="/wiki/Data_remanence" title="Data remanence">retains information</a> for up to several minutes (or even longer, if cooled) after the power has been removed. The <a href="/wiki/Forensic_disk_controller" title="Forensic disk controller">Bress/Menz device</a>, described in US Patent 9,514,789, can accomplish this type of attack.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-46" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-46"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>46<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Similar full disk encryption mechanisms of other vendors and other operating systems, including <a href="/wiki/Linux" title="Linux">Linux</a> and <a href="/wiki/MacOS" title="MacOS">Mac OS X</a>, are vulnerable to the same attack. The authors recommend that computers be powered down when not in physical control of the owner (rather than be left in a <a href="/wiki/Sleep_mode" title="Sleep mode">sleep mode</a>) and that the encryption software be configured to require a password to boot the machine.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ColdBoot2&#95;45-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ColdBoot2-45"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>45<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>On 10 November 2015, Microsoft released a security update to mitigate a security vulnerability in BitLocker that allowed authentication to be bypassed by employing a malicious <a href="/wiki/Kerberos_(protocol)" title="Kerberos (protocol)">Kerberos</a> key distribution center, if the attacker had physical access to the machine, the machine was part of a domain and had no PIN or USB flash drive protection.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-47" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-47"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>47<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li>
<li>BitLocker still does not properly support TPM 2.0 security features which, as a result, can lead to a complete bypass of privacy protection when keys are transmitted over <a href="/wiki/Serial_Peripheral_Interface" title="Serial Peripheral Interface">Serial Peripheral Interface</a> in a motherboard.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-48" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-48"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>48<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup></li></ul>
<p>All these attacks require physical access to the system and are thwarted by a secondary protector such as a USB flash drive or PIN code.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Upholding_Kerckhoffs's_principle"><span id="Upholding_Kerckhoffs.27s_principle"></span>Upholding Kerckhoffs's principle</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=8" title="Edit section: Upholding Kerckhoffs&#039;s principle"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Although the AES encryption algorithm used in BitLocker is in the <a href="/wiki/Public_domain" title="Public domain">public domain</a>, its implementation in BitLocker, as well as other components of the software, are <a href="/wiki/Proprietary_software" title="Proprietary software">proprietary</a>; however, the code is available for scrutiny by Microsoft partners and enterprises, subject to a <a href="/wiki/Non-disclosure_agreement" title="Non-disclosure agreement">non-disclosure agreement</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-49" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-49"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>49<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-50" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-50"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>50<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>According to Microsoft sources,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-51" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-51"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>51<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> BitLocker does not contain an intentionally built-in <a href="/wiki/Backdoor_(computing)" title="Backdoor (computing)">backdoor</a>, so there is no Microsoft-provided way for <a href="/wiki/Law_enforcement" title="Law enforcement">law enforcement</a> to have guaranteed access to the data on a user's drive. In 2006, the <a href="/wiki/Home_Office" title="Home Office">UK Home Office</a> expressed concern over the lack of a backdoor and tried entering into talks with Microsoft to get one introduced.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-52" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-52"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>52<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Microsoft developer and cryptographer <a href="/wiki/Niels_Ferguson" title="Niels Ferguson">Niels Ferguson</a> denied the backdoor request and said, "over my dead body".<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:0&#95;53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-53"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Microsoft engineers have said that United States <a href="/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation" title="Federal Bureau of Investigation">Federal Bureau of Investigation</a> agents also put pressure on them in numerous meetings to add a backdoor, although no formal, written request was ever made; Microsoft engineers eventually suggested that agents should look for the <a href="/wiki/Hard_copy" title="Hard copy">hard copy</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Encryption_key" class="mw-redirect" title="Encryption key">encryption key</a> that the BitLocker program suggests that its users make.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-54" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-54"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>54<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Niels Ferguson's position that "back doors are simply not acceptable"<sup id="cite&#95;ref-:0&#95;53-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-:0-53"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>53<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> is in accordance with <a href="/wiki/Kerckhoffs%27s_principle" title="Kerckhoffs&#39;s principle">Kerckhoffs's principle</a>. Stated by Netherlands-born cryptographer <a href="/wiki/Auguste_Kerckhoffs" title="Auguste Kerckhoffs">Auguste Kerckhoffs</a> in the 19th century, the principle holds that a <a href="/wiki/Cryptosystem" title="Cryptosystem">cryptosystem</a> should be secure, even if everything about the system, except the encryption key, is public knowledge.
</p><p>Since 2014, BitLocker's method and data structure is public knowledge due to reverse engineering; the Linux <a href="/wiki/Comparison_of_disk_encryption_software" title="Comparison of disk encryption software">dislocker</a> program is capable of reading and writing BitLocker-protected drives given the key; since 2020, this can also be done with <a href="/wiki/Cryptsetup" class="mw-redirect" title="Cryptsetup">cryptsetup</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-55" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-55"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>55<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-56" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-56"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>56<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Other_concerns">Other concerns</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=BitLocker&amp;action=edit&amp;section=9" title="Edit section: Other concerns"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Starting with Windows 8 and Windows Server 2012, Microsoft removed the Elephant Diffuser from the BitLocker scheme for no declared reason.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-57" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-57"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>57<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Dan Rosendorf's research shows that removing the Elephant Diffuser had an "undeniably negative impact" on the security of BitLocker encryption against a targeted attack.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-58" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-58"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>58<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Microsoft later cited performance concerns, and noncompliance with the <a href="/wiki/Federal_Information_Processing_Standards" title="Federal Information Processing Standards">Federal Information Processing Standards</a> (FIPS), to justify the diffuser's removal.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-59" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-59"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>59<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Starting with Windows 10 version 1511, however, Microsoft added a new FIPS-compliant <a href="/wiki/Disk_encryption_theory#XTS" title="Disk encryption theory">XTS-AES</a> encryption algorithm to BitLocker.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-Win10New&#95;1-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Win10New-1"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>1<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Starting with Windows 10 version 1803, Microsoft added a new feature called "Kernel Direct Memory access (DMA) Protection" to BitLocker, to protect against <a href="/wiki/DMA_attack" title="DMA attack">DMA attacks</a> via <a href="/wiki/Thunderbolt_3" class="mw-redirect" title="Thunderbolt 3">Thunderbolt 3</a> ports.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-60" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-60"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>60<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-61" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-61"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>61<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> "Kernel Direct Memory access (DMA) Protection" only protects against attacks through Thunderbolt. Direct Memory Access is also possible through <a href="/wiki/PCI_Express" title="PCI Express">PCI Express</a>. In this type of attack an attacker would connect a malicious <a href="/wiki/PCI_Express" title="PCI Express">PCI Express</a> Device,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-62" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-62"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>62<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> which can in turn write directly to the memory and bypass the Windows login. To protect against this type of attack, Microsoft introduced "Virtualization-based Security".<sup id="cite&#95;ref-63" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-63"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>63<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-64" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-64"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>64<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In October 2017, it was reported that a flaw enabled private keys to be inferred from <a href="/wiki/Public_key_cryptography" class="mw-redirect" title="Public key cryptography">public keys</a>, which could allow an attacker to bypass BitLocker encryption when an affected TPM chip is used.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-ars20171016&#95;65-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ars20171016-65"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>65<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> The flaw is the Return of Coppersmith's Attack or <a href="/wiki/ROCA_vulnerability" title="ROCA vulnerability">ROCA vulnerability</a> which is in a code library developed by <a href="/wiki/Infineon" class="mw-redirect" title="Infineon">Infineon</a> and had been in widespread use in security products such as <a href="/wiki/Smartcard" class="mw-redirect" title="Smartcard">smartcards</a> and TPMs. Microsoft released an updated version of the firmware for Infineon TPM chips that fixes the flaw via Windows Update.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-66" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-66"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>66<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In May 2026, it was reported in CVE-2026-45585 that BitLocker protection can be bypassed placing specially crafted FsTx files on a USB drive or EFI partition, also known as YellowKey BitLocker Bypass.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-67" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-67"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>67<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
